mathematicskit.Adam: A quadratic whose two coordinates differ in curvature by a factor of 1000. Fixed-step gradient descent must use a step small enough for the stiff coordinate, so it crawls along the flat one. Adam rescales each coordinate by its root-mean-square gradient and moves both at a similar speed.
Adam on a badly scaled problem
mathematicskit.AdaptiveQuadrature: QUADPACK's adaptive strategy estimates each subinterval's integral two ways and splits only those subintervals where the estimates disagree. AdaptiveQuadrature wraps scipy.integrate.quad (QUADPACK's QAGS). Recording every point at which it samples a sharply peaked integrand shows the evaluations crowding around the peak, and a fixed equally spaced rule needs far more evaluations to match its accuracy.
Adaptive quadrature (QUADPACK): subdividing where it is needed
mathematicskit.AiryResult: Plots Ai and Bi across the turning point x = 0 where y'' = xy switches from oscillation to exponential behaviour, and checks the Wronskian Ai Bi' - Ai' Bi = 1/pi.
The Airy functions Ai and Bi
mathematicskit.AssignmentResult: Assigns workers to jobs at minimum total cost. Brute force would check n! assignments; the Hungarian method solves the problem in polynomial time, and matches brute force on a small instance.
Kuhn's Hungarian method: the assignment problem
mathematicskit.BFGS: The Nelder-Mead simplex method uses function values only. On the Rosenbrock function it needs more function evaluations than BFGS, which uses gradients, but it also works on objectives that have no gradient at all.

On the Rosenbrock function from (-1.2, 1.0), BFGS builds an inverse-Hessian approximation from gradients alone. It needs only a few dozen iterations, as few as Newton's method with the exact Hessian at every step, while gradient descent needs thousands. Near the minimum its convergence is superlinear: the ratio of successive errors tends to zero.
BFGS: Newton-like convergence without second derivatives
mathematicskit.BarnsleyFern: Barnsley's fern is the attractor of just four contractive affine maps, drawn with the chaos game: start anywhere, and at each step apply one of the maps chosen at random with Barnsley's probabilities. Hutchinson's theorem says the fern is the unique set equal to the union of its four images under the maps, which the second figure shows directly.
Barnsley's fern: an iterated function system

mathematicskit.BendixsonResult: If the divergence of a planar vector field keeps one sign on a simply connected region, no closed orbit fits inside it. A damped oscillator passes the test everywhere; the Van der Pol field fails it because its divergence \mu(1 - x^2) changes sign at |x| = 1 -- and indeed its limit cycle must cross those lines.
mathematicskit.Beta: Starting from Bayes's uniform prior, the posterior for an unknown success probability p after k successes in n trials is \mathrm{Beta}(k+1, n-k+1). It narrows around the true value as data accumulate, and its mean is Laplace's rule of succession (k+1)/(n+2).
Bayes's problem: learning a probability from data

mathematicskit.BezoutResult: Euclid's Elements (Book VII, Propositions 1-2) finds the greatest common divisor by repeating \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b) until the remainder vanishes. This script traces the division steps for one pair, recovers Bézout's coefficients ax + by = \gcd(a, b) with extended_gcd, and maps how many steps the algorithm needs: the slowest inputs are consecutive Fibonacci numbers (Lamé, 1844).
mathematicskit.Binomial: Kolmogorov (1933) defined a probability space (\Omega, \mathcal F, P): a sample space \Omega, a collection \mathcal F of events (subsets of \Omega), and a measure P satisfying
Kolmogorov's axioms: events as sets, probability as a measure

Two players stake equal amounts on a game of fair rounds; the first to win a set number of rounds takes the pot. The game is interrupted when player A still needs a wins and player B needs b. How should the pot be split?
Pascal and Fermat's problem of points: dividing the stakes

Many independent trials, each with a tiny chance of success, produce a number of successes that follows a Poisson distribution. Poisson (1837) obtained it as the limit of \mathrm{Binomial}(n, p) with n \to \infty, p \to 0 and the mean np = \mu held fixed:
Poisson's law of rare events: the binomial limit

Bernoulli's "golden theorem" (1713): in n independent trials of an event with probability p, the relative frequency of the event converges to p as n grows. Here a biased coin with p = 0.3 is tossed a million times, and the running fraction of heads homes in on 0.3 while its typical error shrinks like \sqrt{p(1-p)/n}.
Jacob Bernoulli's law of large numbers: frequencies settle down

De Moivre (1733) showed that the binomial distribution, suitably standardized, approaches the normal curve for large n. Laplace (1810) extended this to sums of many independent variables of almost any distribution: the standardized mean Z = (\bar X_n - \mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n) tends to \mathcal N(0, 1), whatever the shape of the summands.
De Moivre-Laplace and the central limit theorem: the bell curve emerges

mathematicskit.BipartiteMatchingResult: Finds a maximum matching in a random bipartite graph with the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm and builds a vertex cover of exactly the same size, as König's theorem guarantees.
mathematicskit.BipartiteMatchingResult.s: Finds a maximum matching in a random bipartite graph with the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm and builds a vertex cover of exactly the same size, as König's theorem guarantees.
mathematicskit.Bisection: Old Babylonian tablets give \sqrt{2} to about six decimal places. The rule Heron of Alexandria later wrote down averages a guess with a divided by the guess, x_{n+1} = \tfrac12(x_n + a/x_n). Bisection needs even less: it halves a bracket [a, b] on which f changes sign, relying only on the intermediate value theorem. This script computes \sqrt{2} both ways and shows the bracket shrinking by exactly half per step, against the Babylonian rule's doubling of correct digits.
The Babylonian square root and bisection
mathematicskit.BootstrapResult: Compares a bootstrap confidence interval for the median (which has no simple closed form) against the parametric t-based interval for the mean, on the same skewed dataset.

Leaves out one observation at a time and recomputes the statistic. For the plug-in variance, the jackknife's bias correction recovers the unbiased n - 1 variance exactly, and for the mean its standard error is exactly the classical s / sqrt(n). For a non-smooth statistic such as the midrange, the jackknife standard error is unreliable and disagrees with the bootstrap's -- one of the shortcomings Efron's bootstrap was designed to overcome.
mathematicskit.BoxCountingResult: Generates the Sierpinski triangle via the chaos game and estimates its box-counting dimension, comparing against the known closed-form value \log 3/\log 2 \approx 1.585.
Box-counting dimension of the Sierpinski triangle

Starts from [0, 1] and repeatedly removes the open middle third of every remaining interval. After n steps there are 2^n intervals of total length (2/3)^n \to 0, yet the limit set is uncountable. Box counting recovers its fractional dimension \log 2/\log 3 \approx 0.631.
Cantor's middle-thirds set and its dimension
mathematicskit.BranchingProcessResult: Each man has 0, 1, or 2 sons with probabilities 0.2, 0.3, 0.5. The extinction probability is the smallest fixed point of the generating function G(s) = 0.2 + 0.3s + 0.5s^2, namely q = 0.4, even though the population grows by 30% per generation on average.
Galton-Watson: the probability a family name dies out
mathematicskit.BrownianMotionResult: Sample paths of standard Brownian motion spread like \sqrt{t}: at time t, W(t) \sim \mathcal N(0, t), so about 95% of paths lie within \pm 2\sqrt t. The quadratic variation \sum (\Delta W)^2 equals t, the signature of a path that is continuous but nowhere differentiable.
mathematicskit.Brusselator: The Brusselator's fixed point (a, b/a) is stable until b crosses b_c = 1 + a^2, where the trace of its Jacobian changes sign and a limit cycle is born: the model chemical reaction starts to oscillate.
mathematicskit.BuffonNeedleResult: A needle as long as the gap between parallel lines crosses a line with probability 2/\pi, so counting crossings estimates \pi. The estimate's error shrinks like 1/\sqrt{n}.
Buffon's needle: estimating pi by dropping needles
mathematicskit.CRTResult: The 3rd-5th-century Chinese text Sunzi Suanjing poses: "There are certain things whose number is unknown. Repeatedly divided by 3, the remainder is 2; by 5 the remainder is 3; by 7 the remainder is 2. What is the number?" -- the original problem the Chinese Remainder Theorem is named for.
mathematicskit.CellularAutomaton: Rule 30 (chaotic) and rule 90 (a discrete Sierpinski triangle) from a single seed cell, plus a glider gun-free Game of Life demonstration using the classic "glider" spaceship.
Elementary cellular automata and Conway's Game of Life
mathematicskit.CellularAutomaton.run: Rule 30 (chaotic) and rule 90 (a discrete Sierpinski triangle) from a single seed cell, plus a glider gun-free Game of Life demonstration using the classic "glider" spaceship.
Elementary cellular automata and Conway's Game of Life
mathematicskit.ChebyshevInterpolant: Chebyshev showed that the polynomial of degree n closest to f in the maximum norm is characterized by an error curve that reaches its peak magnitude n + 2 times with alternating sign. Evgeny Remez's 1934 exchange algorithm finds it by repeatedly levelling the error on a set of reference points. This script computes the best degree-6 approximation to e^x \sin(3x) on [-1, 1] and compares its error with Chebyshev interpolation of the same degree.
Remez's algorithm and best uniform approximation

Chebyshev's least-deviation polynomials suggest placing interpolation nodes at the extrema of T_n(x) = \cos(n \arccos x), which cluster toward the ends of [-1, 1]. At these nodes the Lebesgue constant grows only logarithmically, so the interpolant of Runge's function 1/(1+25x^2) converges as the degree rises. This script shows the node clustering, the degree-20 Chebyshev interpolant, and its error shrinking geometrically.
Chebyshev nodes: the cure for Runge's phenomenon

mathematicskit.CholeskyResult: Cholesky factors a symmetric positive-definite A = L L^T at roughly half the cost of LU, and the factorization succeeding at all (every sqrt argument staying positive) is itself a certificate of positive-definiteness.
mathematicskit.CircleResult: Finds the smallest circle containing a random point cloud with Welzl's algorithm. The optimal circle always passes through two or three of the points.
Sylvester's problem: the smallest enclosing circle
mathematicskit.ClenshawCurtisQuadrature: Compares Clenshaw-Curtis quadrature, which integrates the Chebyshev interpolant, with Gauss-Legendre quadrature on smooth integrands. The two converge at nearly the same rate.
mathematicskit.ClosestPairResult: Finds the closest pair in random point sets by divide and conquer, checks the answer with a k-d tree, and compares the running time with the brute-force comparison of every pair.
Shamos and Hoey: the closest pair of points
mathematicskit.ColoringResult: Draws a map of 20 countries, turns it into a planar graph (one vertex per country, an edge for each shared border), and colors it. Exact backtracking search needs exactly four colors, as Guthrie conjectured and Appel and Haken proved, while the fast greedy heuristic can waste a fifth color on the same map.
The four color theorem: coloring a planar map
mathematicskit.CompositionSeriesResult: Builds composition series for several groups and lists the orders of their simple factors. Different groups of the same order can share the same factors, and the Jordan-Hölder theorem says that every series of one group has the same factors.
Jordan-Hölder: composition series and their factors
mathematicskit.ConfidenceIntervalResult: Compares a bootstrap confidence interval for the median (which has no simple closed form) against the parametric t-based interval for the mean, on the same skewed dataset.

Builds many 95% confidence intervals from repeated samples of a known population, and checks that close to 95% of them actually contain the true parameter -- the frequentist interpretation of "95% confidence."
Confirming a 95% confidence interval's coverage by simulation
mathematicskit.ConjugateGradient: Both are Krylov-subspace iterative solvers that never form a dense factorization of A. Conjugate gradient requires A symmetric positive-definite; GMRES works for any nonsingular A. This script watches both converge and plots the residual-norm history.
mathematicskit.ContinuedFractionResult: Expands pi as a continued fraction and shows how quickly its convergents (355/113 famously accurate to 7 digits) approach the true value.

mathematicskit.CorrelationResult: Simulates parent and child heights in the spirit of Francis Galton's 1880s data: the two are positively correlated, but tall parents have children who are on average less extreme -- "regression toward the mean". Pearson's r measures the strength of that linear relation.
mathematicskit.CubicSpline: A cubic spline is a piecewise cubic through the data with continuous value, first, and second derivatives across nodes. A natural spline sets the curvature to zero at both ends; a clamped spline instead matches prescribed end-slopes. This script fits both to the same data and compares them against a single high-degree interpolating polynomial, which oscillates far more between nodes -- the practical motivation for splines over one global polynomial.

Cayley's 1854 definition treats a group purely as symbols with a binary operation. Here the group of his title, generated by \theta with \theta^n = 1, is written as an abstract FiniteGroup whose elements are just the strings "1", "θ", "θ²", .... Its Cayley table is identical to that of \mathbb{Z}_6, while the non-abelian S_3 of the same order gives a visibly different, non-symmetric table.
Cayley's abstract group and its multiplication table
Checks |G| = |\ker\varphi| \cdot |\operatorname{im}\varphi| for every homomorphism x \mapsto ax from Z_12 to itself, and shows that the sign map on S_4 has the alternating group A_4 as its kernel.

Enumerates every subgroup of Z_12 and confirms each subgroup's order divides 12, and that its left cosets partition the whole group.

Repeated measurements of one quantity scatter around its true value. Gauss (1809) asked which error law makes the arithmetic mean of the measurements the most probable value of the quantity, and found the normal law. This example simulates noisy measurements, compares their errors with the normal curve, and checks that the mean both maximizes the normal error probability and minimizes the sum of squared errors.

Two players stake equal amounts on a game of fair rounds; the first to win a set number of rounds takes the pot. The game is interrupted when player A still needs a wins and player B needs b. How should the pot be split?
Pascal and Fermat's problem of points: dividing the stakes

Many independent trials, each with a tiny chance of success, produce a number of successes that follows a Poisson distribution. Poisson (1837) obtained it as the limit of \mathrm{Binomial}(n, p) with n \to \infty, p \to 0 and the mean np = \mu held fixed:
Poisson's law of rare events: the binomial limit

Poincare sections of the driven Duffing oscillator
mathematicskit.EigenResult: Cauchy's 1829 memoir showed that a real symmetric matrix has only real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so A = V diag(lambda) V^T. Geometrically, the eigenvectors are the principal axes of the quadric x^T A x = 1. A non-symmetric matrix enjoys neither property.
Cauchy's spectral theorem: principal axes of a quadratic form

Power iteration v_{k+1} = A v_k / ||A v_k|| converges to the dominant eigenvector at the rate |lambda_2 / lambda_1| per step (squared for the Rayleigh quotient of a symmetric matrix). Inverse iteration applies the same step to (A - mu I)^{-1} and homes in on the eigenvalue nearest the shift mu, at the much faster rate |lambda - mu| / |lambda' - mu|.
Von Mises power iteration and Wielandt inverse iteration

The 1-D discrete Laplacian tridiag(-1, 2, -1) of size n has eigenvalues 2 - 2 cos(j pi / (n + 1)). Lanczos iteration (through ARPACK) finds a handful of them using only matrix-vector products. In shift-invert mode it handles a sparse n = 100 000 instance, where a dense eigensolver would need 80 GB just to store the matrix.
Lanczos: a few eigenvalues of a very large matrix

mathematicskit.EscapeTimeResult: Iterates the quadratic map z \mapsto z^2 + c from every starting point z_0 of a grid. Points whose orbits stay bounded form the filled Julia set; its boundary, the Julia set, separates the Fatou set, where nearby orbits behave alike, from the region where orbits escape to infinity. Changing c turns the Julia set from a circle into a fractal curve or a disconnected dust.
Fatou and Julia: Julia sets of z -> z^2 + c

Colours every parameter c by how quickly the orbit of z_0 = 0 under z \mapsto z^2 + c escapes. The black region, the Mandelbrot set, is the set of c whose orbit stays bounded -- equivalently, whose Julia set is connected. Zooming into its boundary reveals ever finer detail, including small copies of the whole set.
mathematicskit.ExhaustionResult: Doubles the sides of inscribed and circumscribed regular polygons from 6 to 96, reproducing Archimedes' bounds 3 10/71 < pi < 3 1/7, and shows that the gap shrinks by a factor of four with each doubling.
Archimedes' method of exhaustion: squeezing pi

Galois turned the question "is this equation solvable?" into a question about a group of permutations of its roots. The roots of x^3 - 2 are \sqrt[3]{2}, \sqrt[3]{2}\,\omega and \sqrt[3]{2}\,\omega^2 (with \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}). Complex conjugation swaps the two non-real roots, multiplication by \omega cycles all three, and closing these two permutations under composition gives Galois's group -- the full symmetric group S_3, which is non-abelian.
Galois's permutation groups: S_3 permuting the roots of x^3 - 2
Builds the dihedral group D_4 of the eight symmetries of a square, checks its defining relations, and draws its Cayley table.
Klein's Erlangen program: the symmetry group of a square
Verifies Hamilton's relations i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1 in the quaternion group, shows that it is non-abelian, and prints its multiplication table.

Cayley's 1854 definition treats a group purely as symbols with a binary operation. Here the group of his title, generated by \theta with \theta^n = 1, is written as an abstract FiniteGroup whose elements are just the strings "1", "θ", "θ²", .... Its Cayley table is identical to that of \mathbb{Z}_6, while the non-abelian S_3 of the same order gives a visibly different, non-symmetric table.
Cayley's abstract group and its multiplication table
Checks |G| = |\ker\varphi| \cdot |\operatorname{im}\varphi| for every homomorphism x \mapsto ax from Z_12 to itself, and shows that the sign map on S_4 has the alternating group A_4 as its kernel.
For each prime p dividing a group's order, finds the elements of order p, and checks McKay's refinement that their number is congruent to -1 modulo p.
Cauchy's theorem: elements of prime order

Computes the derived series of the symmetric groups S_2 to S_5. It reaches the trivial group for n <= 4 but stalls at A_5 for n = 5, the group-theoretic reason the general quintic has no formula in radicals.
Abel-Ruffini and solvable groups: why S_5 blocks the quintic
Finds the Sylow 2- and 3-subgroups of the symmetric group S_4 (order 24 = 2^3 * 3) and checks the counting constraints n_p = 1 (mod p) and n_p \mid |G|/p^k.
Finds the normal Klein four-group V_4 inside S_4, forms the quotient S_4/V_4, and shows that it is a non-abelian group of order 6, like S_3.
Hölder's quotient groups: S_4 / V_4 is S_3

Builds composition series for several groups and lists the orders of their simple factors. Different groups of the same order can share the same factors, and the Jordan-Hölder theorem says that every series of one group has the same factors.
Jordan-Hölder: composition series and their factors
Enumerates every subgroup of Z_12 and confirms each subgroup's order divides 12, and that its left cosets partition the whole group.
Lagrange's theorem: subgroup order divides group order

mathematicskit.FixedPointIteration: Old Babylonian tablets give \sqrt{2} to about six decimal places. The rule Heron of Alexandria later wrote down averages a guess with a divided by the guess, x_{n+1} = \tfrac12(x_n + a/x_n). Bisection needs even less: it halves a bracket [a, b] on which f changes sign, relying only on the intermediate value theorem. This script computes \sqrt{2} both ways and shows the bracket shrinking by exactly half per step, against the Babylonian rule's doubling of correct digits.
The Babylonian square root and bisection

Aitken's \Delta^2 process (1926) extrapolates a linearly convergent sequence from three consecutive terms. Applied to the slowly converging Leibniz series for \pi, one pass gains several digits. Steffensen's method (1933) applies the same extrapolation inside a fixed-point iteration, turning the linear convergence of x_{n+1} = \cos x_n into quadratic convergence without any derivative.
Aitken's delta-squared process and Steffensen's method
mathematicskit.FixedPointResult: The nonlinear pendulum \ddot\theta = -\sin\theta has no elementary closed-form solution, but Poincaré's qualitative approach does not need one. Locate the fixed points, classify each from its linearization, and sketch the vector field: the global picture of librating orbits around the centers, rotating orbits above and below, and separatrices joining the saddles follows without solving anything. Integrated trajectories are overlaid only to confirm the prediction.
Poincaré's qualitative method: the pendulum's phase portrait

Poincaré's qualitative theory sorts a planar fixed point into one of four types -- node, saddle, spiral (focus), or center -- using only the eigenvalues of the linearized flow, without solving the equations. The eigenvalues depend only on the Jacobian's trace \tau and determinant \Delta, so every type occupies its own region of the (\tau, \Delta) plane. This script classifies six canonical matrices, draws their phase portraits, and places each one on Poincaré's trace-determinant diagram.
Poincaré's classification of fixed points: nodes, saddles, spirals, centers
mathematicskit.FlowSystem: Lorenz's 1963 convection model \dot x = \sigma(y - x), \dot y = x(\rho - z) - y, \dot z = xy - \beta z is fully deterministic, yet for \sigma = 10, \rho = 28, \beta = 8/3 its orbits wind forever around a butterfly-shaped strange attractor. This script repeats Lorenz's accidental experiment: restart a run from a state rounded to three decimal places, and watch the two forecasts agree for a while, then diverge completely.

Rossler's flow has a single nonlinear term, yet for a = b = 0.2, c = 5.7 it settles onto a chaotic attractor: orbits spiral outward near the plane z \approx 0, are lifted and folded back when x exceeds c, and never exactly repeat. Plotting each loop's maximum of x against the previous one gives a Lorenz-style return map, a thin single-humped curve.

An epidemic grows only if R_0 S_0 > 1, peaks when the susceptible fraction falls to 1/R_0, and burns out before infecting everyone. The simulated peak and final size agree with the closed-form Kermack-McKendrick relations.

With no injected current the model neuron rests at a stable fixed point. Between the two Hopf currents that fixed point is unstable, and the neuron fires repetitively on a relaxation limit cycle that runs along the outer branches of the cubic v-nullcline.

Trajectories starting both inside and outside the eventual limit cycle converge onto the same closed orbit -- the defining property that distinguishes a limit cycle from a linear center (whose orbit amplitude is set entirely by the initial condition).
The Van der Pol limit cycle

If the divergence of a planar vector field keeps one sign on a simply connected region, no closed orbit fits inside it. A damped oscillator passes the test everywhere; the Van der Pol field fails it because its divergence \mu(1 - x^2) changes sign at |x| = 1 -- and indeed its limit cycle must cross those lines.

The Brusselator's fixed point (a, b/a) is stable until b crosses b_c = 1 + a^2, where the trace of its Jacobian changes sign and a limit cycle is born: the model chemical reaction starts to oscillate.

Integrating \dot N = rN(1 - N/K) numerically reproduces Verhulst's closed-form sigmoid exactly: growth looks exponential at first, is fastest at N = K/2, and saturates at the carrying capacity K from any positive starting population.

Predator and prey populations rise and fall periodically, out of phase. Every orbit is closed because the Lotka-Volterra invariant V = \delta x - \gamma\ln x + \beta y - \alpha\ln y is conserved: orbits are its level sets around the coexistence fixed point.

For a stable linear system \dot x = Ax, solving the Lyapunov equation A^T P + PA = -Q gives an energy-like function V(x) = x^T P x whose level sets are ellipses that every trajectory crosses inward -- a proof of stability that never solves the ODE itself.

A thousand oscillators with Lorentzian-distributed natural frequencies stay incoherent for weak coupling. Above the critical coupling K_c = 2\gamma a synchronized cluster forms, and the steady coherence follows Kuramoto's exact result r = \sqrt{1 - K_c/K}.

Kolmogorov's axioms: events as sets, probability as a measure

mathematicskit.GaussSeidel: The three classical stationary iterations on the 1-D Poisson matrix tridiag(-1, 2, -1). Gauss-Seidel contracts the error about twice as fast per sweep as Jacobi, and SOR at Young's optimal relaxation factor is faster by an order of magnitude.
mathematicskit.GaussianQuadrature: Gauss let a quadrature rule choose its sample points as well as its weights. The optimal n nodes turn out to be the roots of the Legendre polynomial P_n, and the resulting rule integrates every polynomial of degree up to 2n-1 exactly -- about twice the degree an equally spaced rule with the same number of points manages. This example shows the nodes and weights from legendre_nodes_and_weights, checks the degree of exactness of GaussianQuadrature, and compares its convergence with the equally spaced trapezoidal rule.
Gaussian quadrature: optimal nodes are exact to degree 2n-1
Compares Clenshaw-Curtis quadrature, which integrates the Chebyshev interpolant, with Gauss-Legendre quadrature on smooth integrands. The two converge at nearly the same rate.

Integrates 1/sqrt(x) and log(x) over [0, 1], whose integrands blow up at 0. The tanh-sinh substitution crowds nodes toward the endpoints with double-exponentially small weights, and converges far faster than Gauss-Legendre quadrature on these integrands.
mathematicskit.GaussianQuadrature.integr: Gauss let a quadrature rule choose its sample points as well as its weights. mathematicskit.Geometric: The number of independent trials up to and including the first success, with success probability p, has mean 1/p and is memoryless: P(X > m + n \mid X > m) = P(X > n).
The geometric distribution: waiting for the first success

mathematicskit.GershgorinResult: Without computing anything but row sums, Gershgorin's theorem traps every eigenvalue in a union of discs centered on the diagonal entries. Shrinking the off-diagonal part shrinks the discs onto the eigenvalues.

mathematicskit.GradientDescent: Compares Polak-Ribiere nonlinear CG against plain gradient descent on the same ill-conditioned quadratic bowl -- CG's conjugate search directions avoid the zig-zagging that slows gradient descent down.
Nonlinear conjugate gradient vs. gradient descent

Gradient descent zig-zags across a narrow, elongated quadratic bowl. Backtracking line search adapts its step length automatically and converges in far fewer iterations than any single fixed step size.
Fixed step vs. backtracking line search on an ill-conditioned bowl

On an ill-conditioned convex quadratic, plain gradient descent reduces the objective gap like O(1/k) until the strongly convex regime kicks in; Nesterov's accelerated gradient, with the same step size, achieves the optimal first-order rate O(1/k^2).

A quadratic whose two coordinates differ in curvature by a factor of 1000. Fixed-step gradient descent must use a step small enough for the stiff coordinate, so it crawls along the flat one. Adam rescales each coordinate by its root-mean-square gradient and moves both at a similar speed.
Adam on a badly scaled problem
mathematicskit.GradientDescentLineSearch: Gradient descent zig-zags across a narrow, elongated quadratic bowl. Backtracking line search adapts its step length automatically and converges in far fewer iterations than any single fixed step size.
Fixed step vs. backtracking line search on an ill-conditioned bowl

On the Rosenbrock function from (-1.2, 1.0), BFGS builds an inverse-Hessian approximation from gradients alone. It needs only a few dozen iterations, as few as Newton's method with the exact Hessian at every step, while gradient descent needs thousands. Near the minimum its convergence is superlinear: the ratio of successive errors tends to zero.
BFGS: Newton-like convergence without second derivatives

f(x, y) = 100(y-x^2)^2 + (1-x)^2 has its minimum f=0 at (1, 1), at the end of a banana-shaped valley along the parabola y = x^2. The walls are steep, but the floor is almost flat, so a method without curvature information finds the valley quickly and then crawls along it.
Rosenbrock's banana function: a narrow curved valley
mathematicskit.Graph: Draws a map of 20 countries, turns it into a planar graph (one vertex per country, an edge for each shared border), and colors it. Exact backtracking search needs exactly four colors, as Guthrie conjectured and Appel and Haken proved, while the fast greedy heuristic can waste a fifth color on the same map.
The four color theorem: coloring a planar map

Reduces Königsberg to four land masses joined by seven bridges and counts the bridges at each land mass. All four counts are odd, so by Euler's argument no walk can cross every bridge exactly once, and an exhaustive search agrees. Removing a single bridge leaves exactly two odd land masses, and a walk over every remaining bridge appears.
Euler and the Seven Bridges of Königsberg

Builds the Turán graph T(n, r), checks that it has no clique of size r + 1, and shows that adding any missing edge creates one. For r = 2 this is Mantel's theorem: a triangle-free graph on n vertices has at most n^2/4 edges.
Turán's theorem: the densest clique-free graphs
Solves Hamilton's 1857 puzzle: travel along the edges of a dodecahedron through all 20 vertices exactly once and return to the start. The same search shows that the Petersen graph has no such cycle.
Finds a maximum matching in a random bipartite graph with the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm and builds a vertex cover of exactly the same size, as König's theorem guarantees.
The classic CLRS flow network: finds the maximum flow from source to sink, and confirms the max-flow min-cut theorem -- the minimum cut's capacity exactly equals the maximum flow value.
Maximum flow and the max-flow min-cut theorem

Ranks the vertices of a small web of links by the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links with probability 0.85 and otherwise jumps to a random page, and shows the convergence of the power iteration.
PageRank: ranking pages by a random surfer
Finds a shortest path across a grid with a wall. With the Manhattan distance as its heuristic, A* reaches the same distance as Dijkstra's algorithm while expanding far fewer vertices.
A* search on a grid with obstacles

Runs Dijkstra's algorithm from one source on a small weighted graph and draws the resulting shortest-path tree. Bellman-Ford gives the same distances there, and takes over on a graph with a negative edge, where Dijkstra's greedy assumption breaks down.
Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm (and when Bellman-Ford is needed)
Computes every shortest-path distance in a weighted graph at once with the Floyd-Warshall algorithm, and checks that it agrees with running Dijkstra's algorithm from every vertex.

Both algorithms find the same minimum spanning tree (same total weight) via very different strategies: Kruskal grows a forest by globally cheapest edge, Prim grows a single tree by locally cheapest edge.
Kruskal's vs. Prim's minimum spanning tree
Counts spanning trees with a single determinant of the reduced Laplacian, and checks the count by brute-force enumeration of edge subsets on a small graph.

Two dense clusters joined by a single bridge edge -- a case where the Fiedler vector's sign cleanly recovers the two clusters, and the small algebraic connectivity reflects how easily the graph is disconnected (by removing just the bridge).
Fiedler's spectral bipartition of a "barbell" graph

mathematicskit.HallResult: Checks Hall's condition on random bipartite graphs and confirms that it holds exactly when a matching covers every left vertex. When it fails, the example prints the subset whose neighbourhood is too small.
mathematicskit.Halley: Edmond Halley's 1694 iteration uses the second derivative as well as the first, stepping to the root of an osculating hyperbola instead of a tangent line. Near a simple root it triples the number of correct digits per step, against Newton's doubling. This script solves x^3 = 2 with both methods from the same starting guess and compares their error histories and empirical convergence orders.
mathematicskit.HermiteInterpolant: Charles Hermite's 1878 interpolant matches both f(x_i) and f'(x_i), so n + 1 nodes fix a polynomial of degree 2n + 1. On the same few nodes it follows \sin far more closely than the Lagrange interpolant, which knows only the values.
Hermite interpolation: matching slopes as well as values
mathematicskit.HomomorphismResult: Checks |G| = |\ker\varphi| \cdot |\operatorname{im}\varphi| for every homomorphism x \mapsto ax from Z_12 to itself, and shows that the sign map on S_4 has the alternating group A_4 as its kernel.
mathematicskit.HornerResult: Horner's 1819 scheme rewrites a_n x^n + \dots + a_0 as nested multiplications, using n multiplications instead of the 2n - 1 of the term-by-term form. Its intermediate values are the coefficients of the quotient p(x) / (x - x_0), which gives the derivative for Newton's method and lets a found root be divided out ("deflation"). This script finds all roots of a quartic that way and compares operation counts.
Horner's method: evaluation, derivative, and deflation
mathematicskit.HypothesisTestResult: With only a handful of measurements, the standardized mean t = (\bar x - \mu_0)/(s/\sqrt n) is not normal: estimating the spread from the same small sample gives it heavier tails. Gosset ("Student", 1908) derived its exact distribution. This example shows the heavy tails, how a normal cutoff misleads for small samples, and the one- and two-sample t-tests built on Student's distribution.
Student's t-distribution and the small-sample t-test

Pearson's chi-square statistic applied two ways: testing whether a die's observed roll counts match a fair-die model (goodness-of-fit), and testing whether two categorical variables in a contingency table are independent.

Compares three fertilizer treatments' effect on plant growth, as in Fisher's Rothamsted field trials. ANOVA splits the total variability into a between-groups and a within-groups sum of squares; their ratio, the F-statistic, tests all group means for equality in one test.

Draws a sample from a Student t distribution with 3 degrees of freedom and compares its empirical CDF with the standard normal CDF. The KS statistic is the largest vertical gap between the two curves.
Rank tests throw away the raw values and keep only their order, so a few extreme observations cannot dominate. With heavy-tailed data they detect a shift that the t-test misses.
mathematicskit.HypothesisTestResult.reje: Pearson's chi-square statistic applied two ways: testing whether a die's observed roll counts match a fair-die model (goodness-of-fit), and testing whether two categorical variables in a contingency table are independent.
mathematicskit.Interpolant: Chebyshev showed that the polynomial of degree n closest to f in the maximum norm is characterized by an error curve that reaches its peak magnitude n + 2 times with alternating sign. Evgeny Remez's 1934 exchange algorithm finds it by repeatedly levelling the error on a set of reference points. This script computes the best degree-6 approximation to e^x \sin(3x) on [-1, 1] and compares its error with Chebyshev interpolation of the same degree.
Remez's algorithm and best uniform approximation

Carl Runge's 1901 example f(x) = 1/(1+25x^2) is smooth on [-1, 1], yet interpolating it at more equally spaced nodes makes the fit worse: oscillations near the endpoints grow without bound as the degree increases. This script shows the overshoot for growing degree, the maximum error blowing up, and the exponentially growing Lebesgue constant of equally spaced nodes that causes it.
Runge's phenomenon: equally spaced interpolation diverges

Chebyshev's least-deviation polynomials suggest placing interpolation nodes at the extrema of T_n(x) = \cos(n \arccos x), which cluster toward the ends of [-1, 1]. At these nodes the Lebesgue constant grows only logarithmically, so the interpolant of Runge's function 1/(1+25x^2) converges as the degree rises. This script shows the node clustering, the degree-20 Chebyshev interpolant, and its error shrinking geometrically.
Chebyshev nodes: the cure for Runge's phenomenon

There is exactly one polynomial of degree \leq n through n+1 distinct points, so LagrangeInterpolant and NewtonDividedDifference -- built from completely different representations (a sum of basis polynomials vs. nested divided differences) -- must produce identical curves. Both are also exact for any polynomial up to the interpolation degree, which this script verifies directly.

Hermite interpolation: matching slopes as well as values

A cubic spline is a piecewise cubic through the data with continuous value, first, and second derivatives across nodes. A natural spline sets the curvature to zero at both ends; a clamped spline instead matches prescribed end-slopes. This script fits both to the same data and compares them against a single high-degree interpolating polynomial, which oscillates far more between nodes -- the practical motivation for splines over one global polynomial.

mathematicskit.IteratedFunctionSystem: Generates the Sierpinski triangle via the chaos game and estimates its box-counting dimension, comparing against the known closed-form value \log 3/\log 2 \approx 1.585.
Box-counting dimension of the Sierpinski triangle
Solves Moran's equation sum r_i^D = 1 for several self-similar sets and compares the answers with box-counting estimates computed from the sets themselves.
Hausdorff and Moran: the similarity dimension

Sierpiński's triangle (1915) removes the middle quarter of a filled triangle and repeats on the three corner triangles; his carpet (1916) removes the middle ninth of a square and repeats on the eight remaining squares. Both limits have zero area and a dimension strictly between 1 and 2. Here both are drawn with the chaos game.

Barnsley's fern is the attractor of just four contractive affine maps, drawn with the chaos game: start anywhere, and at each step apply one of the maps chosen at random with Barnsley's probabilities. Hutchinson's theorem says the fern is the unique set equal to the union of its four images under the maps, which the second figure shows directly.
Barnsley's fern: an iterated function system

mathematicskit.IterativeLinearSolver: Both are Krylov-subspace iterative solvers that never form a dense factorization of A. Conjugate gradient requires A symmetric positive-definite; GMRES works for any nonsingular A. This script watches both converge and plots the residual-norm history.

The three classical stationary iterations on the 1-D Poisson matrix tridiag(-1, 2, -1). Gauss-Seidel contracts the error about twice as fast per sweep as Jacobi, and SOR at Young's optimal relaxation factor is faster by an order of magnitude.
mathematicskit.IterativeRootFinder: Old Babylonian tablets give \sqrt{2} to about six decimal places. The rule Heron of Alexandria later wrote down averages a guess with a divided by the guess, x_{n+1} = \tfrac12(x_n + a/x_n). Bisection needs even less: it halves a bracket [a, b] on which f changes sign, relying only on the intermediate value theorem. This script computes \sqrt{2} both ways and shows the bracket shrinking by exactly half per step, against the Babylonian rule's doubling of correct digits.
The Babylonian square root and bisection

Newton and Raphson's iteration replaces f by its tangent line at the current guess and steps to where that line crosses zero, x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n). This script draws the first tangent steps for f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5 (the cubic Newton himself used as his example) and shows the number of correct digits roughly doubling at every step, i.e. convergence of order 2.
Newton-Raphson's method: tangent lines and quadratic convergence

Edmond Halley's 1694 iteration uses the second derivative as well as the first, stepping to the root of an osculating hyperbola instead of a tangent line. Near a simple root it triples the number of correct digits per step, against Newton's doubling. This script solves x^3 = 2 with both methods from the same starting guess and compares their error histories and empirical convergence orders.

Aitken's \Delta^2 process (1926) extrapolates a linearly convergent sequence from three consecutive terms. Applied to the slowly converging Leibniz series for \pi, one pass gains several digits. Steffensen's method (1933) applies the same extrapolation inside a fixed-point iteration, turning the linear convergence of x_{n+1} = \cos x_n into quadratic convergence without any derivative.
Aitken's delta-squared process and Steffensen's method
mathematicskit.IterativeSolveResult: Both are Krylov-subspace iterative solvers that never form a dense factorization of A. Conjugate gradient requires A symmetric positive-definite; GMRES works for any nonsingular A. This script watches both converge and plots the residual-norm history.

The three classical stationary iterations on the 1-D Poisson matrix tridiag(-1, 2, -1). Gauss-Seidel contracts the error about twice as fast per sweep as Jacobi, and SOR at Young's optimal relaxation factor is faster by an order of magnitude.
mathematicskit.JackknifeResult: Leaves out one observation at a time and recomputes the statistic. For the plug-in variance, the jackknife's bias correction recovers the unbiased n - 1 variance exactly, and for the mean its standard error is exactly the classical s / sqrt(n). For a non-smooth statistic such as the midrange, the jackknife standard error is unreliable and disagrees with the bootstrap's -- one of the shortcomings Efron's bootstrap was designed to overcome.
mathematicskit.JacobiEllipticResult: Plots sn, cn, dn for m = 0.9, showing their real period 4K(m), and uses them to write the exact motion of a large-amplitude pendulum.
Jacobi elliptic functions and the pendulum
mathematicskit.JacobiIteration: The three classical stationary iterations on the 1-D Poisson matrix tridiag(-1, 2, -1). Gauss-Seidel contracts the error about twice as fast per sweep as Jacobi, and SOR at Young's optimal relaxation factor is faster by an order of magnitude.
mathematicskit.KKTResult: Minimizes x^2+y^2 subject to x+y=1. At the constrained optimum (0.5, 0.5) the objective's gradient is parallel to the constraint's gradient, \nabla f = -\lambda \nabla h with \lambda=-1, which is Lagrange's condition. Rewriting the constraint as the inequality x+y \geq 1 gives a Karush-Kuhn-Tucker problem whose multiplier must also be non-negative.
Lagrange multipliers and the KKT conditions
mathematicskit.KnapsackResult: Fills a table of optimal values for every prefix of the items and every capacity, then traces back the chosen items. The table is the dynamic-programming "value function".
Bellman's principle of optimality: the 0/1 knapsack
mathematicskit.KuramotoModel: A thousand oscillators with Lorentzian-distributed natural frequencies stay incoherent for weak coupling. Above the critical coupling K_c = 2\gamma a synchronized cluster forms, and the steady coherence follows Kuramoto's exact result r = \sqrt{1 - K_c/K}.

mathematicskit.LeastSquaresResult: Fits a four-parameter damped cosine to noisy data. The residuals depend nonlinearly on the decay rate and frequency, so the fit needs an iterative method; Levenberg-Marquardt blends gradient descent (far from the solution) with Gauss-Newton (close to it).
mathematicskit.Linear2D: Poincaré's qualitative theory sorts a planar fixed point into one of four types -- node, saddle, spiral (focus), or center -- using only the eigenvalues of the linearized flow, without solving the equations. The eigenvalues depend only on the Jacobian's trace \tau and determinant \Delta, so every type occupies its own region of the (\tau, \Delta) plane. This script classifies six canonical matrices, draws their phase portraits, and places each one on Poincaré's trace-determinant diagram.
Poincaré's classification of fixed points: nodes, saddles, spirals, centers

For a stable linear system \dot x = Ax, solving the Lyapunov equation A^T P + PA = -Q gives an energy-like function V(x) = x^T P x whose level sets are ellipses that every trajectory crosses inward -- a proof of stability that never solves the ODE itself.

mathematicskit.LinearDiophantineResult: Diophantus's Arithmetica asks for whole-number solutions of equations with more unknowns than constraints. For the linear case ax + by = c, integer solutions exist exactly when \gcd(a, b) divides c, and then they form one infinite family spaced evenly along the line. This script solves 12x + 18y = 30, shows that 12x + 18y = 31 has no solution, and plots the integer points on the line.
Diophantus and the linear equation ax + by = c
mathematicskit.LinearProgramResult: Maximize the profit 3x + 5y from two products subject to x + 2y \leq 40 labor-hours and 2x + y \leq 30 units of material. The simplex method starts at the vertex (0, 0) of the feasible polygon and pivots along its edges to an adjacent vertex with a higher profit, until no neighbour improves. The tableau pivots are written out below, and the answer is checked against linear_program.
Dantzig's simplex method: walking the vertices of a production LP

The LP relaxation of an integer program can have a fractional optimum that rounding does not repair. Branch and bound (Land and Doig, 1960) finds the true integer optimum; here it is at a different vertex from the relaxation's.
Branch and bound: integer versus relaxed optimum
mathematicskit.LogisticGrowth: Integrating \dot N = rN(1 - N/K) numerically reproduces Verhulst's closed-form sigmoid exactly: growth looks exponential at first, is fastest at N = K/2, and saturates at the carrying capacity K from any positive starting population.
mathematicskit.LorenzSystem: Lorenz's 1963 convection model \dot x = \sigma(y - x), \dot y = x(\rho - z) - y, \dot z = xy - \beta z is fully deterministic, yet for \sigma = 10, \rho = 28, \beta = 8/3 its orbits wind forever around a butterfly-shaped strange attractor. This script repeats Lorenz's accidental experiment: restart a run from a state rounded to three decimal places, and watch the two forecasts agree for a while, then diverge completely.

mathematicskit.MSTResult: Both algorithms find the same minimum spanning tree (same total weight) via very different strategies: Kruskal grows a forest by globally cheapest edge, Prim grows a single tree by locally cheapest edge.
Kruskal's vs. Prim's minimum spanning tree
mathematicskit.MarkovChain: A Markov chain moves between states with probabilities that depend only on the current state, not on how it got there, so the whole process is described by one transition matrix. In gambler's ruin, a gambler with capital i (out of a target N) makes fair even-money bets until reaching 0 (ruin) or N (target); the capital after each bet is a Markov chain on the states 0..N with two absorbing ends. Both the absorption probabilities and the expected number of steps have simple closed forms for a fair game, used here to check the numerical solve.
Markov chains: gambler's ruin as an absorbing chain

mathematicskit.MaxFlowResult: The classic CLRS flow network: finds the maximum flow from source to sink, and confirms the max-flow min-cut theorem -- the minimum cut's capacity exactly equals the maximum flow value.
Maximum flow and the max-flow min-cut theorem
mathematicskit.MaximumLikelihoodResult: Repeated measurements of one quantity scatter around its true value. Gauss (1809) asked which error law makes the arithmetic mean of the measurements the most probable value of the quantity, and found the normal law. This example simulates noisy measurements, compares their errors with the normal curve, and checks that the mean both maximizes the normal error probability and minimizes the sum of squared errors.

Fits an exponential and a gamma distribution to the same skewed data by maximum likelihood, and plots the exponential model's log-likelihood as a function of its scale: the curve peaks exactly at the sample mean, the closed-form MLE.

Repeatedly tests the true null hypothesis "the normal mean is 0" with the likelihood-ratio statistic 2(l1 - l0). Wilks's theorem says the statistic's null distribution approaches chi-square with one degree of freedom, the number of parameters the null hypothesis fixes.
Wilks's theorem and the likelihood-ratio test
mathematicskit.MaximumLikelihoodResult.a: Fits an exponential and a gamma distribution to the same skewed data by maximum likelihood, and plots the exponential model's log-likelihood as a function of its scale: the curve peaks exactly at the sample mean, the closed-form MLE.
mathematicskit.MinimaxResult: Chebyshev showed that the polynomial of degree n closest to f in the maximum norm is characterized by an error curve that reaches its peak magnitude n + 2 times with alternating sign. Evgeny Remez's 1934 exchange algorithm finds it by repeatedly levelling the error on a set of reference points. This script computes the best degree-6 approximation to e^x \sin(3x) on [-1, 1] and compares its error with Chebyshev interpolation of the same degree.
Remez's algorithm and best uniform approximation

Evgeny Remez's 1934 exchange algorithm finds it by repeatedly levelling the error on a set of reference points. This script computes the best degree-6 approximation to e^x \sin(3x) on [-1, 1] and compares its error with Chebyshev interpolation of the same degree.
Remez's algorithm and best uniform approximation
mathematicskit.MonteCarloResult: Ulam and von Neumann's idea: replace an exact calculation by an average over random samples. For U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 1),
The Monte Carlo method: estimating an integral by random sampling
mathematicskit.NelderMead: The Nelder-Mead simplex method uses function values only. On the Rosenbrock function it needs more function evaluations than BFGS, which uses gradients, but it also works on objectives that have no gradient at all.
mathematicskit.NesterovAcceleratedGradie: On an ill-conditioned convex quadratic, plain gradient descent reduces the objective gap like O(1/k) until the strongly convex regime kicks in; Nesterov's accelerated gradient, with the same step size, achieves the optimal first-order rate O(1/k^2).
mathematicskit.NewtonDividedDifference: There is exactly one polynomial of degree \leq n through n+1 distinct points, so LagrangeInterpolant and NewtonDividedDifference -- built from completely different representations (a sum of basis polynomials vs. nested divided differences) -- must produce identical curves. Both are also exact for any polynomial up to the interpolation degree, which this script verifies directly.
mathematicskit.NewtonDividedDifference.e: There is exactly one polynomial of degree \leq n through n+1 distinct points, so LagrangeInterpolant and NewtonDividedDifference -- built from completely different representations (a sum of basis polynomials vs. nested divided differences) -- must produce identical curves. Both are also exact for any polynomial up to the interpolation degree, which this script verifies directly.
mathematicskit.NewtonMethod: On the Rosenbrock function from (-1.2, 1.0), BFGS builds an inverse-Hessian approximation from gradients alone. It needs only a few dozen iterations, as few as Newton's method with the exact Hessian at every step, while gradient descent needs thousands. Near the minimum its convergence is superlinear: the ratio of successive errors tends to zero.
BFGS: Newton-like convergence without second derivatives
mathematicskit.NewtonRaphson: Newton and Raphson's iteration replaces f by its tangent line at the current guess and steps to where that line crosses zero, x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n). This script draws the first tangent steps for f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5 (the cubic Newton himself used as his example) and shows the number of correct digits roughly doubling at every step, i.e. convergence of order 2.
Newton-Raphson's method: tangent lines and quadratic convergence

Edmond Halley's 1694 iteration uses the second derivative as well as the first, stepping to the root of an osculating hyperbola instead of a tangent line. Near a simple root it triples the number of correct digits per step, against Newton's doubling. This script solves x^3 = 2 with both methods from the same starting guess and compares their error histories and empirical convergence orders.
mathematicskit.Nonlinear2D: The nonlinear pendulum \ddot\theta = -\sin\theta has no elementary closed-form solution, but Poincaré's qualitative approach does not need one. Locate the fixed points, classify each from its linearization, and sketch the vector field: the global picture of librating orbits around the centers, rotating orbits above and below, and separatrices joining the saddles follows without solving anything. Integrated trajectories are overlaid only to confirm the prediction.
Poincaré's qualitative method: the pendulum's phase portrait

mathematicskit.NonlinearConjugateGradien: Compares Polak-Ribiere nonlinear CG against plain gradient descent on the same ill-conditioned quadratic bowl -- CG's conjugate search directions avoid the zig-zagging that slows gradient descent down.
Nonlinear conjugate gradient vs. gradient descent
mathematicskit.Normal: Kolmogorov (1933) defined a probability space (\Omega, \mathcal F, P): a sample space \Omega, a collection \mathcal F of events (subsets of \Omega), and a measure P satisfying
Kolmogorov's axioms: events as sets, probability as a measure
A Gamma(shape=1, rate) distribution is exactly an Exponential(rate); increasing the shape parameter builds up a sum of exponentials.
The gamma distribution generalizes the exponential

De Moivre (1733) showed that the binomial distribution, suitably standardized, approaches the normal curve for large n. Laplace (1810) extended this to sums of many independent variables of almost any distribution: the standardized mean Z = (\bar X_n - \mu)/(\sigma/\sqrt n) tends to \mathcal N(0, 1), whatever the shape of the summands.
De Moivre-Laplace and the central limit theorem: the bell curve emerges
P(|X-\mu| \geq k\sigma) \leq 1/k^2 holds for any distribution with finite variance. Comparing it with exact tails shows how conservative a universal bound has to be.
Chebyshev's inequality: one bound for every distribution

Rossler's flow has a single nonlinear term, yet for a = b = 0.2, c = 5.7 it settles onto a chaotic attractor: orbits spiral outward near the plane z \approx 0, are lifted and folded back when x exceeds c, and never exactly repeat. Plotting each loop's maximum of x against the previous one gives a Lorenz-style return map, a thin single-humped curve.

An epidemic grows only if R_0 S_0 > 1, peaks when the susceptible fraction falls to 1/R_0, and burns out before infecting everyone. The simulated peak and final size agree with the closed-form Kermack-McKendrick relations.

With no injected current the model neuron rests at a stable fixed point. Between the two Hopf currents that fixed point is unstable, and the neuron fires repetitively on a relaxation limit cycle that runs along the outer branches of the cubic v-nullcline.

Trajectories starting both inside and outside the eventual limit cycle converge onto the same closed orbit -- the defining property that distinguishes a limit cycle from a linear center (whose orbit amplitude is set entirely by the initial condition).
The Van der Pol limit cycle

If the divergence of a planar vector field keeps one sign on a simply connected region, no closed orbit fits inside it. A damped oscillator passes the test everywhere; the Van der Pol field fails it because its divergence \mu(1 - x^2) changes sign at |x| = 1 -- and indeed its limit cycle must cross those lines.

The Brusselator's fixed point (a, b/a) is stable until b crosses b_c = 1 + a^2, where the trace of its Jacobian changes sign and a limit cycle is born: the model chemical reaction starts to oscillate.

A thousand oscillators with Lorentzian-distributed natural frequencies stay incoherent for weak coupling. Above the critical coupling K_c = 2\gamma a synchronized cluster forms, and the steady coherence follows Kuramoto's exact result r = \sqrt{1 - K_c/K}.
mathematicskit.OptimizeResult: Compares Polak-Ribiere nonlinear CG against plain gradient descent on the same ill-conditioned quadratic bowl -- CG's conjugate search directions avoid the zig-zagging that slows gradient descent down.
Nonlinear conjugate gradient vs. gradient descent

Minimizes a convex quadratic over the triangle \{x \geq 0,\ x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1\} without ever projecting onto it. Each step solves a linear program, whose solution is a vertex, and moves toward that vertex. The Frank-Wolfe gap certifies how far the objective is from optimal.
Frank-Wolfe: optimization over the probability simplex

Fiacco and McCormick's sequential unconstrained minimization replaces \min x^2+y^2 subject to x+y=1 with the unconstrained problems \min x^2+y^2+\mu(x+y-1)^2 for growing \mu. Each penalized minimizer violates the constraint slightly, and the violation shrinks like 1/\mu as the minimizers approach the constrained optimum (0.5, 0.5).
The quadratic penalty method: a sequence of unconstrained problems

The Nelder-Mead simplex method uses function values only. On the Rosenbrock function it needs more function evaluations than BFGS, which uses gradients, but it also works on objectives that have no gradient at all.

Gradient descent zig-zags across a narrow, elongated quadratic bowl. Backtracking line search adapts its step length automatically and converges in far fewer iterations than any single fixed step size.
Fixed step vs. backtracking line search on an ill-conditioned bowl

On an ill-conditioned convex quadratic, plain gradient descent reduces the objective gap like O(1/k) until the strongly convex regime kicks in; Nesterov's accelerated gradient, with the same step size, achieves the optimal first-order rate O(1/k^2).

A quadratic whose two coordinates differ in curvature by a factor of 1000. Fixed-step gradient descent must use a step small enough for the stiff coordinate, so it crawls along the flat one. Adam rescales each coordinate by its root-mean-square gradient and moves both at a similar speed.
Adam on a badly scaled problem

On the Rosenbrock function from (-1.2, 1.0), BFGS builds an inverse-Hessian approximation from gradients alone. It needs only a few dozen iterations, as few as Newton's method with the exact Hessian at every step, while gradient descent needs thousands. Near the minimum its convergence is superlinear: the ratio of successive errors tends to zero.
BFGS: Newton-like convergence without second derivatives

Minimizes a quadratic using only noisy gradient observations. With Robbins and Monro's step sizes a_k = a_0/(k+1), the noise averages out and the error shrinks like 1/\sqrt{k}. A constant step size instead stalls at a noise floor.
Robbins-Monro: stochastic gradient descent with decaying steps

f(x, y) = 100(y-x^2)^2 + (1-x)^2 has its minimum f=0 at (1, 1), at the end of a banana-shaped valley along the parabola y = x^2. The walls are steep, but the floor is almost flat, so a method without curvature information finds the valley quickly and then crawls along it.
Rosenbrock's banana function: a narrow curved valley
mathematicskit.PadeApproximant: Henri Padé's 1892 thesis organized rational approximations p(x)/q(x) that match a function's Taylor series as far as possible. The Taylor series of \log(1 + x) diverges for x > 1, but the Padé approximants built from the same coefficients keep converging well beyond it.
Padé approximants beyond the radius of convergence
mathematicskit.PageRankResult: Ranks the vertices of a small web of links by the stationary distribution of a random surfer who follows links with probability 0.85 and otherwise jumps to a random page, and shows the convergence of the power iteration.
PageRank: ranking pages by a random surfer
mathematicskit.PellResult: Fermat's 1657 challenge: solve x^2 - Dy^2 = 1 in integers. The continued fraction of \sqrt D always yields the fundamental solution (Lagrange, 1768), but its size is wildly erratic -- for D = 61 it is x = 1766319049, while D = 60 needs only x = 31. This script reproduces Fermat's D = 61 case, generates further solutions from the fundamental one, and plots the fundamental x for every non-square D \le 120.
mathematicskit.PenaltyMethod: Fiacco and McCormick's sequential unconstrained minimization replaces \min x^2+y^2 subject to x+y=1 with the unconstrained problems \min x^2+y^2+\mu(x+y-1)^2 for growing \mu. Each penalized minimizer violates the constraint slightly, and the violation shrinks like 1/\mu as the minimizers approach the constrained optimum (0.5, 0.5).
The quadratic penalty method: a sequence of unconstrained problems
mathematicskit.PermutationGroup: Counts two-colored necklaces (up to rotation) and bracelets (up to rotation and reflection) by averaging fixed points, and checks each count against direct orbit enumeration.

Galois turned the question "is this equation solvable?" into a question about a group of permutations of its roots. The roots of x^3 - 2 are \sqrt[3]{2}, \sqrt[3]{2}\,\omega and \sqrt[3]{2}\,\omega^2 (with \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}). Complex conjugation swaps the two non-real roots, multiplication by \omega cycles all three, and closing these two permutations under composition gives Galois's group -- the full symmetric group S_3, which is non-abelian.
Galois's permutation groups: S_3 permuting the roots of x^3 - 2
Builds the dihedral group D_4 of the eight symmetries of a square, checks its defining relations, and draws its Cayley table.
Klein's Erlangen program: the symmetry group of a square

Cayley's 1854 definition treats a group purely as symbols with a binary operation. Here the group of his title, generated by \theta with \theta^n = 1, is written as an abstract FiniteGroup whose elements are just the strings "1", "θ", "θ²", .... Its Cayley table is identical to that of \mathbb{Z}_6, while the non-abelian S_3 of the same order gives a visibly different, non-symmetric table.
Cayley's abstract group and its multiplication table
Checks |G| = |\ker\varphi| \cdot |\operatorname{im}\varphi| for every homomorphism x \mapsto ax from Z_12 to itself, and shows that the sign map on S_4 has the alternating group A_4 as its kernel.
For each prime p dividing a group's order, finds the elements of order p, and checks McKay's refinement that their number is congruent to -1 modulo p.
Cauchy's theorem: elements of prime order

Computes the derived series of the symmetric groups S_2 to S_5. It reaches the trivial group for n <= 4 but stalls at A_5 for n = 5, the group-theoretic reason the general quintic has no formula in radicals.
Abel-Ruffini and solvable groups: why S_5 blocks the quintic
Finds the Sylow 2- and 3-subgroups of the symmetric group S_4 (order 24 = 2^3 * 3) and checks the counting constraints n_p = 1 (mod p) and n_p \mid |G|/p^k.
Finds the normal Klein four-group V_4 inside S_4, forms the quotient S_4/V_4, and shows that it is a non-abelian group of order 6, like S_3.
Hölder's quotient groups: S_4 / V_4 is S_3

Builds composition series for several groups and lists the orders of their simple factors. Different groups of the same order can share the same factors, and the Jordan-Hölder theorem says that every series of one group has the same factors.
Jordan-Hölder: composition series and their factors

Production codes add Hessenberg reduction and Francis's shifts; the result is what scipy.linalg.schur returns.

Both factor A = Q R, but Householder reflections stay orthogonal to machine precision even for ill-conditioned A, while classical Gram-Schmidt can lose orthogonality badly -- modified Gram-Schmidt is a partial (but not complete) remedy. mathematicskit.RootResult: Old Babylonian tablets give \sqrt{2} to about six decimal places. The rule Heron of Alexandria later wrote down averages a guess with a divided by the guess, x_{n+1} = \tfrac12(x_n + a/x_n). Bisection needs even less: it halves a bracket [a, b] on which f changes sign, relying only on the intermediate value theorem. This script computes \sqrt{2} both ways and shows the bracket shrinking by exactly half per step, against the Babylonian rule's doubling of correct digits.
The Babylonian square root and bisection

Newton and Raphson's iteration replaces f by its tangent line at the current guess and steps to where that line crosses zero, x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n). This script draws the first tangent steps for f(x) = x^3 - 2x - 5 (the cubic Newton himself used as his example) and shows the number of correct digits roughly doubling at every step, i.e. convergence of order 2.
Newton-Raphson's method: tangent lines and quadratic convergence

Edmond Halley's 1694 iteration uses the second derivative as well as the first, stepping to the root of an osculating hyperbola instead of a tangent line. Near a simple root it triples the number of correct digits per step, against Newton's doubling. This script solves x^3 = 2 with both methods from the same starting guess and compares their error histories and empirical convergence orders.

Aitken's \Delta^2 process (1926) extrapolates a linearly convergent sequence from three consecutive terms. Applied to the slowly converging Leibniz series for \pi, one pass gains several digits. Steffensen's method (1933) applies the same extrapolation inside a fixed-point iteration, turning the linear convergence of x_{n+1} = \cos x_n into quadratic convergence without any derivative.
Aitken's delta-squared process and Steffensen's method

Plotting each loop's maximum of x against the previous one gives a Lorenz-style return map, a thin single-humped curve.

mathematicskit.SVDResult: kappa_2(A) = sigma_max / sigma_min bounds how much a relative perturbation of the data can grow in the solution of A x = b, whichever algorithm solves it: expect to lose about log10(kappa) digits. The same number explains why least squares through the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b is fragile -- kappa(A^T A) = kappa(A)^2 -- while QR works with kappa(A) itself.

Truncating the SVD A = U diag(S) V^T to its k largest singular values gives the best rank-``k`` approximation of A: its error is sqrt(sigma_{k+1}^2 + ...) in the Frobenius norm and sigma_{k+1} in the spectral norm, and no other rank-``k`` matrix does better. The SVD itself comes from numpy.linalg.svd (LAPACK's stable bidiagonalization route, not the eigendecomposition of A^T A).
Eckart-Young: the best low-rank approximation from the SVD

mathematicskit.UnconstrainedOptimizer: Compares Polak-Ribiere nonlinear CG against plain gradient descent on the same ill-conditioned quadratic bowl -- CG's conjugate search directions avoid the zig-zagging that slows gradient descent down.
Nonlinear conjugate gradient vs. gradient descent

The Nelder-Mead simplex method uses function values only. On the Rosenbrock function it needs more function evaluations than BFGS, which uses gradients, but it also works on objectives that have no gradient at all.

Gradient descent zig-zags across a narrow, elongated quadratic bowl. Backtracking line search adapts its step length automatically and converges in far fewer iterations than any single fixed step size.
Fixed step vs. backtracking line search on an ill-conditioned bowl

On an ill-conditioned convex quadratic, plain gradient descent reduces the objective gap like O(1/k) until the strongly convex regime kicks in; Nesterov's accelerated gradient, with the same step size, achieves the optimal first-order rate O(1/k^2).

A quadratic whose two coordinates differ in curvature by a factor of 1000. Fixed-step gradient descent must use a step small enough for the stiff coordinate, so it crawls along the flat one. Adam rescales each coordinate by its root-mean-square gradient and moves both at a similar speed.
Adam on a badly scaled problem

On the Rosenbrock function from (-1.2, 1.0), BFGS builds an inverse-Hessian approximation from gradients alone. It needs only a few dozen iterations, as few as Newton's method with the exact Hessian at every step, while gradient descent needs thousands. Near the minimum its convergence is superlinear: the ratio of successive errors tends to zero.
BFGS: Newton-like convergence without second derivatives

f(x, y) = 100(y-x^2)^2 + (1-x)^2 has its minimum f=0 at (1, 1), at the end of a banana-shaped valley along the parabola y = x^2. The walls are steep, but the floor is almost flat, so a method without curvature information finds the valley quickly and then crawls along it.
Rosenbrock's banana function: a narrow curved valley

If the divergence of a planar vector field keeps one sign on a simply connected region, no closed orbit fits inside it. A damped oscillator passes the test everywhere; the Van der Pol field fails it because its divergence \mu(1 - x^2) changes sign at |x| = 1 -- and indeed its limit cycle must cross those lines.

Galois turned the question "is this equation solvable?" into a question about a group of permutations of its roots. The roots of x^3 - 2 are \sqrt[3]{2}, \sqrt[3]{2}\,\omega and \sqrt[3]{2}\,\omega^2 (with \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}). Complex conjugation swaps the two non-real roots, multiplication by \omega cycles all three, and closing these two permutations under composition gives Galois's group -- the full symmetric group S_3, which is non-abelian.
Galois's permutation groups: S_3 permuting the roots of x^3 - 2

Galois turned the question "is this equation solvable?" into a question about a group of permutations of its roots. The roots of x^3 - 2 are \sqrt[3]{2}, \sqrt[3]{2}\,\omega and \sqrt[3]{2}\,\omega^2 (with \omega = e^{2\pi i/3}). Complex conjugation swaps the two non-real roots, multiplication by \omega cycles all three, and closing these two permutations under composition gives Galois's group -- the full symmetric group S_3, which is non-abelian.

mathematicskit.geometry.polygon_area: Euclid's theory of area (Elements I.35-41) rests on two facts: parallelograms on the same base and between the same parallels are equal in area (I.35), and so are triangles (I.37), each triangle being half of the parallelogram (I.41). Sliding the top side along its parallel line changes every shape but, as the shoelace formula in polygon_area confirms, never the area.
Euclid's Elements, Book I: equal areas between parallels

mathematicskit.linalg.ConjugateGradient: Both are Krylov-subspace iterative solvers that never form a dense factorization of A. Conjugate gradient requires A symmetric positive-definite; GMRES works for any nonsingular A. This script watches both converge and plots the residual-norm history.
mathematicskit.linalg.EigenResult: Cauchy's 1829 memoir showed that a real symmetric matrix has only real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so A = V diag(lambda) V^T. Geometrically, the eigenvectors are the principal axes of the quadric x^T A x = 1. A non-symmetric matrix enjoys neither property.
Cauchy's spectral theorem: principal axes of a quadratic form

Power iteration v_{k+1} = A v_k / ||A v_k|| converges to the dominant eigenvector at the rate |lambda_2 / lambda_1| per step (squared for the Rayleigh quotient of a symmetric matrix). Inverse iteration applies the same step to (A - mu I)^{-1} and homes in on the eigenvalue nearest the shift mu, at the much faster rate |lambda - mu| / |lambda' - mu|.
Von Mises power iteration and Wielandt inverse iteration

The 1-D discrete Laplacian tridiag(-1, 2, -1) of size n has eigenvalues 2 - 2 cos(j pi / (n + 1)). Lanczos iteration (through ARPACK) finds a handful of them using only matrix-vector products. In shift-invert mode it handles a sparse n = 100 000 instance, where a dense eigensolver would need 80 GB just to store the matrix.
Lanczos: a few eigenvalues of a very large matrix
mathematicskit.linalg.GMRES: Both are Krylov-subspace iterative solvers that never form a dense factorization of A. Conjugate gradient requires A symmetric positive-definite; GMRES works for any nonsingular A. This script watches both converge and plots the residual-norm history.
mathematicskit.linalg.GaussSeidel: The three classical stationary iterations on the 1-D Poisson matrix tridiag(-1, 2, -1). Gauss-Seidel contracts the error about twice as fast per sweep as Jacobi, and SOR at Young's optimal relaxation factor is faster by an order of magnitude.
mathematicskit.linalg.GershgorinResult: Without computing anything but row sums, Gershgorin's theorem traps every eigenvalue in a union of discs centered on the diagonal entries. Shrinking the off-diagonal part shrinks the discs onto the eigenvalues.

mathematicskit.linalg.LUResult: Gaussian elimination, with its multipliers stored in L and the eliminated rows in U, factors P A = L U. The script reuses the factorization to solve multiple right-hand sides and compute the determinant, both far cheaper than refactoring from scratch each time.
mathematicskit.linalg.QRResult: Factor A_k = Q_k R_k and multiply back in reverse order, A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k = Q_k^T A_k Q_k. Every iterate is similar to A, and the subdiagonal entries decay like |lambda_{i+1} / lambda_i|^k, so the iterates converge to an upper triangular Schur form with the eigenvalues on the diagonal. Production codes add Hessenberg reduction and Francis's shifts; the result is what scipy.linalg.schur returns.
The QR algorithm and the Schur form

Both factor A = Q R, but Householder reflections stay orthogonal to machine precision even for ill-conditioned A, while classical Gram-Schmidt can lose orthogonality badly -- modified Gram-Schmidt is a partial (but not complete) remedy. This is the textbook motivation for preferring Householder in production numerical software.
mathematicskit.linalg.SOR: The three classical stationary iterations on the 1-D Poisson matrix tridiag(-1, 2, -1). Gauss-Seidel contracts the error about twice as fast per sweep as Jacobi, and SOR at Young's optimal relaxation factor is faster by an order of magnitude.
mathematicskit.linalg.SVDResult: kappa_2(A) = sigma_max / sigma_min bounds how much a relative perturbation of the data can grow in the solution of A x = b, whichever algorithm solves it: expect to lose about log10(kappa) digits. The same number explains why least squares through the normal equations A^T A x = A^T b is fragile -- kappa(A^T A) = kappa(A)^2 -- while QR works with kappa(A) itself.
Turing's condition number: how much a linear system amplifies error

Truncating the SVD A = U diag(S) V^T to its k largest singular values gives the best rank-``k`` approximation of A: its error is sqrt(sigma_{k+1}^2 + ...) in the Frobenius norm and sigma_{k+1} in the spectral norm, and no other rank-``k`` matrix does better. The SVD itself comes from numpy.linalg.svd (LAPACK's stable bidiagonalization route, not the eigendecomposition of A^T A).
Eckart-Young: the best low-rank approximation from the SVD

mathematicskit.linalg.core.SchurResult: Factor A_k = Q_k R_k and multiply back in reverse order, A_{k+1} = R_k Q_k = Q_k^T A_k Q_k. Every iterate is similar to A, and the subdiagonal entries decay like |lambda_{i+1} / lambda_i|^k, so the iterates converge to an upper triangular Schur form with the eigenvalues on the diagonal. Production codes add Hessenberg reduction and Francis's shifts; the result is what scipy.linalg.schur returns.

mathematicskit.linalg.cramer_solve: Cramer's rule gives every unknown as a ratio of two determinants, x_i = det(A_i) / det(A). It is exact in theory but needs n + 1 determinants, each an O(n^3) factorization, so its cost grows like n^4 against elimination's n^3.
mathematicskit.linalg.eigen_general: Cauchy's 1829 memoir showed that a real symmetric matrix has only real eigenvalues and an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, so A = V diag(lambda) V^T. Geometrically, the eigenvectors are the principal axes of the quadric x^T A x = 1. A non-symmetric matrix enjoys neither property.

mathematicskit.linalg.inverse_iteration: Power iteration v_{k+1} = A v_k / ||A v_k|| converges to the dominant eigenvector at the rate |lambda_2 / lambda_1| per step (squared for the Rayleigh quotient of a symmetric matrix). Inverse iteration applies the same step to (A - mu I)^{-1} and homes in on the eigenvalue nearest the shift mu, at the much faster rate |lambda - mu| / |lambda' - mu|.

mathematicskit.linalg.is_symmetric_posit: Cholesky factors a symmetric positive-definite A = L L^T at roughly half the cost of LU, and the factorization succeeding at all (every sqrt argument staying positive) is itself a certificate of positive-definiteness.
mathematicskit.linalg.jacobi_spectral_ra: The three classical stationary iterations on the 1-D Poisson matrix tridiag(-1, 2, -1). Gauss-Seidel contracts the error about twice as fast per sweep as Jacobi, and SOR at Young's optimal relaxation factor is faster by an order of magnitude.
mathematicskit.linalg.lanczos_eigsh: The 1-D discrete Laplacian tridiag(-1, 2, -1) of size n has eigenvalues 2 - 2 cos(j pi / (n + 1)). Lanczos iteration (through ARPACK) finds a handful of them using only matrix-vector products. In shift-invert mode it handles a sparse n = 100 000 instance, where a dense eigensolver would need 80 GB just to store the matrix.

Truncating the SVD A = U diag(S) V^T to its k largest singular values gives the best rank-``k`` approximation of A: its error is sqrt(sigma_{k+1}^2 + ...) in the Frobenius norm and sigma_{k+1} in the spectral norm, and no other rank-``k`` matrix does better. mathematicskit.number_theory.BezoutResul: Euclid's Elements (Book VII, Propositions 1-2) finds the greatest common divisor by repeating \gcd(a, b) = \gcd(b, a \bmod b) until the remainder vanishes.
